Issued at 255 PM EDT Tue Aug 4 2026

Rest of Today-Tonight...Offshore (southwesterly) flow across the 
Florida peninsula between a stalled front/cut-off mid-level low 
over the Deep South and the Bermuda High continues one last day, 
ushering along the west coast sea breeze while slowing the east 
coast breeze, which has developed from the Cape south. Isolated to
scattered showers and lightning storms marching northeast have 
developed inland, and a few have popped up along the east coast 
sea breeze, some of which have slid off the boundary and offshore.
Expect a usual high moisture summer time storm evolution, with 
coverage of showers and storms increasing through the rest of the 
afternoon, becoming scattered to numerous and peaking as the sea 
breezes and outflow boundaries collides over East Central Florida.
A little bit of dry air has found its way into the lower-levels 
from near the Cape to Lake Kissimmee or so southward, which is 
inhibiting convection some, but could also enhance downdrafts and 
produce wind gusts up 55 mph. To the north the saturated 
atmosphere and water loading could still produce gusts 40-50 mph. 
Other storms hazards will be frequent lightning and torrential 
rainfall. Storms and heavy showers that get hung up on boundaries,
especially along the sea breeze collision, could become nearly 
stationary and delivery a quick 2-3" of rainfall, and there is a 
very low chance (10% or less) for locally high amounts over 4", 
that could lead to minor flooding of low-lying and poor drainage 
areas. Near normal temperatures with afternoon highs in the 
U80-L90s, resulting in peak afternoon heat indices around 100. 

Wednesday-Thursday...We settle back into an onshore flow regime 
as the Bermuda High shifts west towards the eastern seaboard, 
quickly lifting the ridge axis through Florida Wednesday, then 
north of the area by Thursday. Moisture remains above normal 
Wednesday in the weakening southerly flow, then bands of 
relatively lower moisture begin to arrive Thursday in the easterly
flow, but overall still staying near to above normal. Despite the
high overall moisture, drier air in the low-levels Wednesday cuts
back rain chances closer to normal, with the highest chances 
(50-70%) shifting towards the interior as the sea breeze is able 
to push farther inland, and lower chances (20-40%) along the 
coast. For Thursday will have to see how the moisture banding sets
up, but for now forecast calls for a slight uptick in rain 
chances (40-60% along the coast and 50-70% inland). Storms will be
capable of the usual threats, gusty winds to 50 mph, occasional 
to frequent lightning, and torrential downpours. Temperatures 
creep up a degree or two, but remain near to slightly below normal
in the U80s-L90s. 

Friday-Saturday...An inverted trough from the tropics is expected
to approach Florida as it slides along the southern flank of the 
Bermuda high, but there is considerable disagreement in track and 
sharpness. The last few runs, the GFS suite has favored a stronger
surface high, tracking the feature across Florida into the Gulf, 
while the ECM suite has favored a weaker high which recurves the 
system near to offshore the coast. The former could lead to 
banding of heavy rainfall across the peninsula, while the latter 
would limit heavy rainfall to the coast or keep it offshore. Both 
are dependent how sharp the trough becomes, with a sharper trough 
supporting banding of heavy rainfall, and the risk decreasing the
weaker the feature stays. However, all scenarios are likely to 
produce rough surf and increase the threat of life-threatening 
rip currents at the beaches as onshore flow increases. Given the 
spread, broad above normal rain and storm chances are maintained 
in the forecast. Otherwise, not much change in temperatures which 
remain near normal, though tick up a degree or two Saturday.

Sunday-Monday (Previous Discussion)...From Sunday into early next
week, cluster analysis shows strong agreement that the Bermuda 
high will flatten and stretch westward over the Gulf and Florida. 
This would likely nudge the surface high pressure axis southward, 
perhaps reaching very close to our latitude by Monday. Somewhat 
drier air, associated with an approaching Saharan Air Layer (SAL),
may impinge on South Florida in about a week. Guidance largely 
agrees that the surge of moisture associated with the 
aforementioned wave will lift northward and away from Central and 
South Florida by Sunday and especially Monday. However, moisture 
values should only tick down to near-normal values for mid-August.
With a robust sea breeze circulation expected, scattered storms 
(30-60%) should still form each day - with the greatest coverage 
over the interior.

As deep-layer ridging parks over Florida, temperatures may trend a
bit hotter, into the low and mid 90s. This will be accompanied by
very muggy conditions.
